newsitem.title: FRANCE: French reflect ahead of Sunday parliamentary vote.
newsitem.headline: French reflect ahead of Sunday parliamentary vote.

text.p: The campaign drums fell silent in France on Saturday, eve of an election in which the centre-right is seeking a new mandate despite high unemployment and painful austerity.

Politicians were barred from television and radio from midnight Friday, giving the country's 39 million voters a day to ponder which of 6,389 candidates to choose in Sunday's first phase of the vote for the 577-seat National Assembly.

The election, with a run-off round on June 1, will either renew President Jacques Chirac's centre-right government until the end of his seven-year term in 2002 or make him a virtual lame duck in an uneasy "cohabitation" with the left.

Gambling his presidency by calling the vote 10 months early after promptings from deeply unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe, Chirac has urged "a new elan" to let France push ahead with European integration, the single currency and free market reforms.

He made a final veiled plug for his allies at an informal European Union summit in the Netherlands, saying he saw a "revolution" in Europe over a growing acceptance of a need for a social model to protect citizens from unemployment and poverty.

The opposition Socialists, campaigning to "Change the Future", have accused Chirac of grovelling to financial markets with fiscal austerity and say he has forgotten his pledges to lead a fight for jobs.

If elected, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin promises to create 700,000 youth jobs and cut the working week to 35 hours from 39 with no loss of pay. He also says he will not impose any extra austerity to qualify for the single currency from 1999.

Opinion surveys published before a polls blackout a week ago showed the centre-right was likely to cling to power, but many voters were undecided and the left was within striking distance of an upset.
"Everything remains possible," the daily Le Parisien said in a front-page headline. "The surprise vote," Liberation said.

The first round will only be a pointer to the final result and Juppe has said no clear trend may emerge. Only candidates winning at least 50 percent will be elected outright, leaving most of the seats to June 1 run-offs.

Polling stations are open from 8 a.m. (0600 GMT) with forecasts of the results, including likely seats in the Assembly after the run-offs, from polling institutes at the close at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT). Most results are due during the evening.

Campaigning has been lacklustre, stirring fears of high abstention. Newspapers have not noted the usual surge in pre-election sales and some surveys have shown rising numbers of undecided voters as polling day nears.
"The campaign has not aroused voters' passions," said Pascal Perrineau, a leading sociologist. "Neither the left nor the right has been able to come up with seductive proposals."

"The right has campaigned behind Alain Juppe on the theme 'we must have a change to change nothing'," he told France Info radio, while the left was campaigning on themes too similar to those rejected by voters in 1993.
The first round score of the far-right National Front led by Jean-Marie Le Pen could also be significant.

The left would be helped if a large number of Front candidates win the 12.5 percent of regstered voters needed to reach the run-off. Front voters generally turn to conservatives in constituencies where their own candidate is eliminated.

"The true danger is him," the daily France-Soir said in a front-page headline alongside a photograph of Le Pen. "And them," it added by a photograph of two riverbank anglers, clearly representing abstentions.
In a final pitch to voters, Juppe said that, if Chirac was forced to "cohabit" with a leftist prime minister, France would be weakened abroad and major economic decisions paralysed.

Jospin warned voters to expect more austerity and a flare-up of social unrest if they re-elected the centre-right. He urged voters to punish the right for unemployment and stop it "monopolising power" for five years.
